# Affine contacts of ordinary maximal-depth roots
mixed-integer convex sets. It gives OC when all positive measured
fibers have the same ordinary raw maximal depth. It does not assert
that a useful contact set retains all the mass in a general body.

The joint own-depth-root concavity, uniqueness of the ordinary deepest
point, and equality rigidity are already proved and independently
audited in the archive. The new step here uses affine sampled upper
contacts of that potential and the occupied-parity strict-face theorem.
The atom weights are the actual ordinary maximal depths, not fiber
volumes. This distinction gives a sharper retained-mass inequality.

## 1. Ordinary definitions and needed facts

For a full-dimensional compact convex body K in R^r, r>=1, let

    D_K(x)=inf_{|u|=1} |K intersect {v:u.(v-x)>=0}|,
    A(K)=max_{x in K} D_K(x),     m(K)=A(K)^(1/r).

Volumes here are r-dimensional. The ordinary deepest point is denoted
g(K). These definitions apply in an affine r-plane using its intrinsic
Euclidean measure and directions. Translation between parallel affine
planes leaves all definitions unchanged.

The function D_K is continuous on K. Indeed cap volume is jointly
continuous in (u,x) by dominated convergence, since the limiting
hyperplane has zero r-volume, and the sphere is compact. Boundary
points have depth zero by a supporting hyperplane; interior points
have positive depth by an interior ball and compactness of directions.
Consequently A(K)>0 is attained in the interior. Opposite through-point
caps partition K up to a null hyperplane, giving A(K)<=|K|/2.

The deepest point is unique. Here is the short complete argument,
including the only local regularity fact it needs. At an interior
point x, if u is a minimizing cap direction, then the centroid of the
section K intersect {u.(v-x)=0} is x. For r=1 this is immediate. For
r>=2, translate x to zero, write u as the last coordinate vector, and
perturb its direction to u+t a with a perpendicular to u. Fubini along
vertical lines gives the cap-volume derivative

    integral_{K intersect u-perp} a.v dH_(r-1)(v).

The difference quotient is bounded by |a.v| on the bounded projection
of K. Except on the boundary of the proper section, which is null in
its plane, its vertical interval has zero strictly between its two
endpoints. Thus dominated convergence justifies the derivative without
smoothness of K. Minimality makes the derivative zero for every a,
so the section centroid is zero.

Now suppose two distinct interior points x0,x1 have the same maximal
depth A. At their midpoint x choose an attaining direction u. Every
cap through x has mass at least A, by ordinary quasiconcavity: its
threshold is between the two endpoint thresholds. If u.x0 differs
from u.x1, the endpoint with larger threshold has strictly smaller cap
volume than the cap through x, because every level strictly between
two interior levels has a positive section. Since the latter cap
has mass A, this contradicts that endpoint's depth. If the thresholds
are equal, the same section is active at both endpoints; its centroid
would be both x0 and x1, again a contradiction. This proves uniqueness.

For convex-compatible fibers the following inclusion proves the
own-depth-root concavity. If (1-t)K0+tK1 is contained in Kt and
xt=(1-t)x0+t x1, then for every common direction u,

    (1-t)[K0 intersect {u.v>=u.x0}]
      +t[K1 intersect {u.v>=u.x1}]
        subset Kt intersect {u.v>=u.xt}.

Brunn--Minkowski and then the infimum over u imply

    D_Kt(xt)^(1/r)
        >=(1-t)D_K0(x0)^(1/r)+t D_K1(x1)^(1/r).    (2)

In particular

    m(Kt)>=(1-t)m(K0)+t m(K1).                       (3)

If equality holds in (3), apply (2) to the endpoint deepest points.
Their interpolated point has depth at least A(Kt), hence exactly
A(Kt). Uniqueness therefore gives the exact identity

    g(Kt)=(1-t)g(K0)+t g(K1).                       (4)

This derivation of (4) needs no separate equality classification of
body shapes. It must not be interpreted as a weaker zero-slack regime:
the independently audited stronger archive theorem proves that equality
in (3), for positive endpoint coefficients and full-dimensional bodies,
also forces Kt=(1-t)K0+tK1 and positively homothetic endpoint bodies.
Conversely equality of the compatible fiber-volume roots forces those
same conclusions and hence equality in (3). Thus the two exact
midpoint zero-slack regimes coincide. Their sampled affine upper
contact sets can nevertheless differ away from equality.

## 2. A general transfer from marked graph atoms to actual fiber volume

Let I be a finite index set with distinct base points z_i in R^n.
Let K_i be full-dimensional bodies in R^r, let x_i be an interior
point of K_i, and choose constants

    0<c_i<=D_Ki(x_i)<|K_i|.

Give the finite graph T={(z_i,x_i):i in I} atom weights c_i. Suppose
y=(z_j,x_j) is a weighted alpha-center of T in the full ambient space,
where alpha>0. Then the raw halfspace depth of y in the actual fiber
union is at least alpha. If the minimal face F of conv(T) containing
y has c(F)>alpha, then that actual depth is strictly greater than alpha.
No convex compatibility or affine graph assumption is needed here.

The non-strict assertion is immediate and includes every oblique cap:
whenever a containing halfspace includes a graph atom (z_i,x_i), its
fiber trace has volume at least c_i. The included graph atoms have
total weight at least alpha. A pure base-normal cap includes their
whole fibers and gives the same bound.

For the strict assertion suppose a sequence of containing caps has
mass tending to alpha. Move each boundary to y, which only decreases
mass and retains the lower bound. Pure base-normal caps have mass at
least rho alpha, where rho=min_i |K_i|/c_i>1, so they cannot form this
sequence after discarding finitely many members. Normalize each
remaining continuous normal to length one and write its fiber-relative
threshold as

    t_(l,i)=-a_l.(z_i-z_j)-u_l.(x_i-x_j),  |u_l|=1.

Pass to a subsequence with u_l convergent, the finite included-atom
set J={i:t_(l,i)<=0} constant, and every t_(l,i) convergent in the
extended real line. For finite limiting thresholds, cap volumes
converge by dominated convergence, and for infinite limits boundedness
gives zero or full volume. Each i in J contributes at least c_i, and
the atomic center property gives sum_J c_i>=alpha. Equality of the
limiting total to alpha forces

    sum_J c_i=alpha,
    t_i=0 for every i in J,
    limiting fiber cap mass zero for i outside J.   (5)

The middle statement follows because a negative threshold strictly
increases a through-x_i cap, as x_i is interior; a threshold minus
infinity gives full volume, also strictly larger than c_i. For i
outside J, zero limiting mass requires

    t_i>=h_(K_i-x_i)(u)>0

or t_i=plus infinity. Thus its thresholds are eventually bounded
below by a positive constant.

Because y lies in the relative interior of F, it has a convex
representation using EVERY graph atom in F with strictly positive
coefficients lambda_i. To obtain such a representation, for each
listed atom move a small distance from y in the opposite direction
while staying in F, represent that new point by vertices of F, and
average the resulting representations of y. Hence

    sum_{i in F} lambda_i t_(l,i)=0 for every l.

Terms from J tend to zero by (5); all terms outside J are nonnegative
and any such term in F stays bounded positively away from zero.
Therefore F is contained in J. This contradicts
c(F)>alpha=sum_J c_i and proves strictness of the infimum itself.

The same proof works for fibers whose intrinsic direction spaces are
one common r-dimensional linear space V. Divide the entire ambient
normal by the length of its projection onto V. Only that projected
normal, now of length one, is used as the convergent direction in the
intrinsic cap-volume limits. Retain the FULL normalized continuous
normal in every offset against x_i-x_j: its V-perpendicular component
can diverge if the affine fiber planes are translated nonaffinely.
The extended threshold subsequence still exists, and the exact ambient
graph barycenter identity still makes their weighted sum zero. No
perpendicular offset is discarded. When the original projection onto
V is zero, every included graph atom has its entire fiber included, so
the rho alpha argument again excludes that case from an equality sequence.
No strict assertion for varying intrinsic direction spaces is inferred
from this normalized-normal proof.

## 3. Main full-dimensional contact theorem

Let C be a compact convex set in R^n times R^d, d>=1, with at least
one positive-volume integer fiber. Let P consist of all integer bases
with nonempty fiber K_z. It is finite. Put

    A_z=A(K_z), m_z=A_z^(1/d), g_z=g(K_z)

on positive-volume fibers, and set A_z=m_z=0 on other fibers.
The deepest point g_z is used only on positive fibers.

Choose an affine function ell on the base space such that

    ell(z)>=m_z for EVERY z in P.

Define its positive contact set

    Q={z in P:m_z=ell(z)>0},

and suppose Q is nonempty. Let k_Q count its occupied integer parity
classes and let B_Q=sum_{z in Q}A_z. Then some actual point
y=(z,g_z), z in Q, has raw mixed depth at least

    B_Q/k_Q >= Gamma_d [sum_{z in Q}|K_z|]/k_Q.      (6)

If |Q|>k_Q, the first inequality for the actual raw depth is strict.
More exactly, strictness holds unless the lifted contact graph
T_Q={(z,g_z):z in Q} consists of k_Q equally weighted vertices, with
weights A_z. The exceptional finite-graph description is only an
exception to the proved strictness mechanism; it does not by itself
assert equality of actual mixed depth, because other fibers may help.

**Proof.** If z,w in Q have the same parity, their integer midpoint
h belongs to P by convexity of C. Its fiber contains (K_z+K_w)/2
and has positive volume. Equation (3) and the affine majorant imply

    m_h >= (m_z+m_w)/2 = ell(h) >= m_h.

Every term is equal, and the common value is positive. Hence h is
in Q, and (4) gives g_h=(g_z+g_w)/2. Thus the actual lifted graph
T_Q is midpoint-closed for every same-parity pair, with k_Q labels.

Apply the finite labeled midpoint theorem in
`candidate 58dcf29bfb78a573`
to graph weights A_z. It provides a weighted B_Q/k_Q graph center,
which is an actual single point (z,g_z). Section 2 transfers its
atomic bound to the actual union of contact fibers, and hence to the
full original measured source. Its strict-face refinement and the
strict transfer give the stated strictness alternatives. Finally
ordinary Grunbaum gives A_z>=Gamma_d |K_z| term by term. QED.

The contact set itself is lattice-complete:

    Q=conv(Q) intersect Z^n.

Indeed if h is an integer convex combination of points of Q, the
same cap inclusion and Brunn--Minkowski argument for a finite convex
combination gives m_h>=sum lambda_z m_z=ell(h). Convexity places its
fiber in C, so h belongs to P and the majorant gives equality. The
value is positive, so h belongs to Q. This completeness fact is not
needed in the lifted proof; the midpoint-label version is what avoids
assuming that the map z->g_z is affine.

## 4. Intrinsic contact theorem, including zero-measure fibers

Now let C and S satisfy the task statement, let q=dim_H(S), and first
assume q>=1. A finite union of compact convex integer fibers has
Hausdorff dimension equal to the maximum of their affine dimensions.
Let P_+ denote the fibers of affine dimension q. Each has finite
positive intrinsic q-volume V_z and all other fibers have zero H_q
measure. Thus

    M=H_q(S)=sum_{z in P_+}V_z,     0<M<infinity.

Use the intrinsic definitions A_z,m_z=A_z^(1/q),g_z on these fibers;
put A_z=m_z=0 on other nonempty integer fibers. An affine sampled
majorant ell and its positive contact set Q are defined as before.
Then some actual y=(z,g_z), z in Q, satisfies

    H_q(S intersect H)>=B_Q/k_Q
        >=Gamma_q [sum_{z in Q}V_z]/k_Q              (7)

for EVERY closed ambient halfspace H containing y.

Here is the additional geometric check required before using intrinsic
Brunn--Minkowski. If two positive q-dimensional integer fibers have
the same parity, their midpoint Minkowski sum is contained in another
integer fiber. The direction space of its affine hull is the sum of
their two q-dimensional direction spaces. Since no integer fiber has
dimension greater than q, these spaces must agree and the midpoint
fiber has the same direction space. We can consequently identify all
three affine q-planes by translations with one Euclidean q-space.
Equations (2)--(4) apply in that space, with exactly the intrinsic
volumes used in the statement. This proves same-parity lifted graph
midpoint closure. The finite graph center theorem applies unchanged.

For transfer, an ambient halfspace containing a marked point either
restricts to a genuine halfspace of that fiber's affine q-plane or
contains that entire fiber. In both cases it captures at least A_z.
All relevant intrinsic fiber measures therefore sum exactly as in
Section 2's non-strict argument. No common direction space across
different parity classes is required for (7). The strict conclusion
from Section 3 is asserted here only if all contact fibers share one
q-direction space, for the reason stated at the end of Section 2.

The intrinsic contact set is also lattice-complete. At an integer
convex combination of positive contact bases, the Minkowski sum of
all positively weighted fibers lies in an integer fiber of dimension
at most q. Therefore all participating q-direction spaces coincide;
finite Brunn--Minkowski gives the same proof as in Section 3.

If q=0, every nonempty integer fiber is a singleton, and H_0(S)
counts those points. The actual graph is midpoint-closed for every
same-parity pair directly by convexity and the singleton fibers.
The finite graph theorem with unit weights supplies an actual point
of depth at least |S|/k, where k<=2^n is its occupied-parity count.
No zero-th root or undefined exponent is used in this case.

## 5. Equal own maximal depths: an OC corollary

Suppose q>=1 and every positive intrinsic q-dimensional integer fiber
has the same ordinary raw maximal depth A_*>0. Take ell identically
A_*^(1/q). It majorizes all sampled m_z, including the zero values,
and Q=P_+. Equation (7) gives an actual point y with

    H_q(S intersect H)>=|P_+| A_*/k
      >=Gamma_q H_q(S)/k
      >=Gamma_d H_q(S)/2^n

for every containing closed ambient halfspace. Here k<=2^n and q<=d.
The sequence Gamma_r=(r/(r+1))^r is decreasing in r>=1: the derivative
of t log(t/(t+1)) is -log(1+1/t)+1/(t+1)<0. Together with Gamma_0=1,
this verifies the last constant comparison, including d>=q.

The q=0 argument above already gives the same OC conclusion with the
stronger constant 2^(-n). When n=0 the sole integer base has its own
ordinary deepest point and the same reasoning reduces to ordinary
Grunbaum. When d=0 only q=0 occurs. These arguments retain all boundary
fibers carrying the intrinsic measure and always produce a point of S.

In the common-direction case q>=1 the raw contact bound is strict
whenever |P_+|>k. This is strict OC as well. The exact finite-graph
exception described in Section 3 is not an equality classification
for arbitrary bodies or arbitrary zero-volume fibers.

## 6. What the contact theorem does not imply

An affine majorant exists, for example the constant maximum of m_z,
but it may touch only a small part of the original measured mass.
Equation (6) uses B_Q, not sum_{all z}A_z. Summing the guarantees of
different contact sets would select different centers and is invalid
without an additional proved simultaneous-selection mechanism.

The archived exact source
`candidate 0549d69dcd95de34` disproves the
unconditional assertion max raw mixed depth>=2^(-n)sum_z A_z.
There is no conflict: its unequal own maxima do not all belong to one
affine contact set. Nor does this theorem assert that the deepest-point
graph is globally affine. It uses only exact midpoint identities on
the chosen contact set, in the actual ambient graph.

Even optimizing over every affine sampled majorant need not make the
retained bound reach OC. There is a three-fiber rational example.
Let n=1,d=2, T=conv(0,e1,e2), V=|T|, Gamma=4/9, and take

    C=conv({-1} times (3T/4), {0} times T,
           {1} times (3T/4)).

These are its exact integer fibers, since their radius profile is
concave. Their maximal-depth roots are the common factor sqrt(Gamma V)
times (3/4,1,3/4). An affine majorant cannot touch both endpoint bases:
it would have value 3/4 times that factor at the middle, below its
actual value. Thus a nonempty contact set is a singleton or two adjacent
bases. A singleton has k_Q=1 and B_Q<=Gamma V. Two adjacent bases
have k_Q=2 and

    B_Q/k_Q=(25/32)Gamma V.

The constant majorant touching only the middle attains Gamma V, so
the largest of all contact bounds is exactly Gamma V. But the OC
target for the full source is

    (Gamma/2)M=(Gamma/2)(17V/8)=(17/16)Gamma V.

This strictly larger target is therefore not a consequence of taking
the best numerical retained-contact bound alone. This example rejects
that proposed extra inference, not the contact theorem or OC.
